userGuidanceHistory.guidance: More than 9.16 crore enterprises are now registered on the Udyam portal, up from 1.65 crore in April 2023, together employing over 40 crore people. When the Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development (Amendment) Bill, 2026 cleared the Rajya Sabha on 3 August and the Lok Sabha on 7 August, Parliament rewrote the operating manual for that constituency for the first time in nearly two decades.  I spent twenty years at ICICI Bank before moving to the NBFC side of this business, and that shapes how I read the amendment. In a large bank, an MSME arrives as a file: a balance sheet, a bureau score, a collateral valuation. At a lender like ours, the same enterprise arrives as a person in a tier-three town, often with no audited accounts and no credit history worth the name. The distance between those two versions of the same business is where India’s MSME credit problem has always lived. What matters in the 2026 amendment is not any single clause but the shift in intent. The 2006 Act was built to recognise MSMEs. The 2026 amendment is built to make them resilient.  Cash flow first Ask a small business owner what keeps them awake, and the answer is rarely demand. It is money earned but not yet received. Delayed payments from large buyers, corporate and government alike, have quietly drained the liquidity of otherwise healthy enterprises, forcing them to borrow simply to bridge the gap between work done and payment made.  The amended law sets timelines where the old framework offered none. Mediation must conclude within 90 days, unresolved disputes must move to arbitration within 30 days, and an award must follow within 90 days of pleadings. It also closes the loophole that made winning meaningless: where a challenge to an award drags past six months, courts must release at least half the awarded amount to the supplier in the meantime. A mediated settlement or arbitral award can now be recovered as an arrear of land revenue through the district collector.  Central Public Sector Enterprises must now settle their MSME invoices through the Trade Receivables Discounting System, the RBI-authorised platform that converts unpaid invoices into cash. TReDS volumes have already grown from roughly ₹40,000 crore in 2022-23 to about ₹3.47 lakh crore in 2025-26. For a sector where a delayed receivable can mean a missed payroll, predictability in the payment cycle is not a technicality. It is oxygen.  Room to grow The amendment also moves the power to set investment and turnover thresholds from statute to government notification. On paper this sounds procedural. In practice it removes a trap.  Under legislated ceilings, a successful enterprise could outgrow its category within a year and abruptly lose the benefits that helped it grow: priority-sector credit, procurement preferences, guarantee cover. I have watched promoters hold back an expansion, or split a business across entities, simply to stay under a threshold. That is a policy failure, not an entrepreneurial one. Thresholds can now be recalibrated without waiting for a fresh Act of Parliament, so that scaling up is rewarded rather than penalised. Alongside this, conviction-based penalties give way to graded civil ones, which makes formalisation feel less like a risk.  Visibility is the real constraint Udyam registration becomes permanent, free, voluntary and digital. This may be the provision with the longest tail. The biggest barrier to affordable credit for a small enterprise is not risk. It is invisibility. A business that exists only in cash and informal ledgers is difficult to underwrite, however sound it may be.  Our founder and Managing Director, Jitendra Tanwar, has lived both sides of that sentence. He began at seventeen, selling tractors to farmers in the villages around Jaipur and explaining loan terms to buyers who had never seen a sanction letter. Namdev Finvest today manages over ₹1,829 crore in assets across 137 branches in nine states, serving more than 46,000+ borrowers. The lesson he built the institution around is a simple one: the enterprises the formal system cannot see are not the ones it should avoid. They are the ones nobody has looked at properly.  A verifiable digital identity linked to income-tax and GST records changes that equation. It lets lenders read genuine cash flows, extend collateral-light working capital, and price risk fairly. Formalisation is not an end. It is the on-ramp to capital.  The work that begins now Several provisions become operational only once the rules and notifications follow, and the real test is implementation: how quickly Facilitation Councils clear disputes, how far TReDS spreads beyond the mandated CPSEs, how consistently recovery is enforced on the ground. A well-drafted law delivers value only when it reaches the enterprise in a small town, not merely the well-advised firm in a metro.  That last mile is where the responsibility sits for lenders committed to India’s underserved businesses. Legislation can set the rules of the game; it cannot, on its own, put working capital in the hands of a first-generation entrepreneur. If the 2006 Act taught India to count its small businesses, the 2026 amendment challenges us to back them.  Sahil Taneja is Chief Business Officer at Namdev Finvest, an RBI-registered NBFC focused on MSME, rural and green lending across nine states. He spent two decades at ICICI Bank across MSME lending, retail assets, branch banking and priority-sector lending before joining the company.
